slides.0.title: Bergerac and the Dordogne
slides.0.subtitle: Bordeaux's eastern neighbour: red, white, noble rot and sweet wines
slides.1.title: The Bergerac family
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Bergerac and Côtes de Bergerac
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Bergerac AOC dates from 1936 and Côtes de Bergerac from 1995; the latter has stricter rules and more structure (Dordogne tourism, Cellar Tours)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Varieties
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Reds are mainly blends of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc; whites use Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon and Muscadelle (Cellar Tours)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Conflicting area figures
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Cellar Tours gives both 1,200 and 12,000 ha on one page; the tourism board lists about 7,000 ha for Bergerac and Côtes de Bergerac, so area and AOC counts (7 or 17) are not tested
slides.1.content: Bergerac is the everyday base, with Côtes de Bergerac above it.
slides.2.title: Reds: Pécharmant and Montravel
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Pécharmant
slides.2.highlights.0.content: AOC 1946; about 450 ha and about 45 producers; Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Malbec; powerful, age-worthy reds (Dordogne tourism)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Montravel
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Haut-Montravel, Montravel dry white and Côtes de Montravel were recognised in 1937, and Montravel Rouge in 2001; plateau soils are boulbène, flint and iron crust
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Climate
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Cellar Tours: more continental than Bordeaux, with colder winters and hotter summers; Wine Folly says Bergerac is slightly warmer than the rest of the region
slides.2.content: Pécharmant is the most prized red within Bergerac.
slides.3.title: Sweet wine: Monbazillac
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Scale and varieties
slides.3.highlights.0.content: AOC 1936; about 2,000 ha per Wine With Seth but 2,320 ha per the tourism board (they differ); Sémillon is over 70% with Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle in support
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Noble rot and picking
slides.3.highlights.1.content: All fruit must be botrytised and mechanical harvesting is banned, with hand picking in successive tries; classic wines need at least 45 g/L and Sélection de Grains Nobles at least 85 g/L (Wine With Seth)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: History
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Around 1080 Benedictine monks of the Abbey of Saint-Martin in Périgueux planted the first vines (dry wines then); replanting on southern slopes began around 1495 after the Hundred Years' War (Wine With Seth)
slides.3.content: Monbazillac is described as the world's largest appellation devoted solely to botrytised sweet wines (Wine With Seth).
slides.4.title: Small sweet appellations and neighbours
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Saussignac
slides.4.highlights.0.content: AOC 2005; about 20 ha; Sauvignon, Sémillon, Muscadelle and Chenin; honey and candied-apricot aromas with about 12 months of ageing (Dordogne tourism)
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Rosette
slides.4.highlights.1.content: AOC 1946; about 40 ha; a medium-sweet white forgotten after phylloxera and revived in the 1960s (Dordogne tourism)
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Côtes de Duras
slides.4.highlights.2.content: AOC 1937; about 1,250 ha; in Lot-et-Garonne on the border of Bordeaux and Bergerac; Chenin and Mauzac are possible for sweet whites (Dordogne tourism)
slides.4.content: Sweet wines here are less famous than Sauternes but far friendlier in price.
